title: `--sdnotify=healthy` holds pod lock while waiting for healthy; other containers in the pod can't be created and `pod inspect` hangs
body:
### Issue Description

When a Quadlet pod member container starts with `Notify=healthy`, its `podman start/run` holds the pod lock until the container is healthy. This results in `podman run/start --pod <same pod>` and `podman pod inspect` blocking (`stop` and `ps` would too).

There is no timeout for the healthy wait (it ends on a healthy state or container exit). If the health check depends on another container in the same pod (i.e. a `Notify=healthy` health check sidecar that probes a primary app container), everything hangs until systemd `TimeoutStartSec` kills both.

It seems that this happens because (looking at 5.8.9):
  - [`Container.Start`](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/blob/v5.8.9/libpod/container_api.go#L88-L105) takes `pod.lock` and holds it through `startNoPodLock` into [`waitForHealthy`](https://github.com/podman-container-tools/podman/blob/v5.8.9/libpod/container_internal.go#L1331-L1361)
 - `waitForHealthy` only releases the container lock

### Steps to reproduce the issue

This minimal repro creates a pod and starts a container (which will be waiting on a healthcheck). It uses `--health-interval=disable` so we can manually trigger the healthcheck (vs. a systemd timer).

```sh
podman pod create --name p1
podman create --pod p1 --name a1 --sdnotify=healthy --health-cmd=/bin/true --health-retries=1 --health-interval=disable docker.io/library/alpine sleep infinity
podman start a1 &  # waiting for a1 to be healthy; health check doesn't run until manually triggered below
sleep 2
time timeout 20 podman run -d --pod p1 --name b1 docker.io/library/alpine sleep infinity; echo "exit: $?"
time timeout 10 podman pod inspect p1 > /dev/null; echo "exit: $?"
podman healthcheck run a1  # a1 is now healthy
wait  # the `podman start a1` above returns
time podman run -d --pod p1 --name b2 docker.io/library/alpine sleep infinity; echo "exit: $?"
podman pod rm -f -t 0 p1
```

### Describe the results you received

- Our `run --pod` for container b1 times out after 20s with `exit: 124`; `pod inspect` also times out after 10s
- After the health check completes (`healthcheck run a1`), `run --pod` for b2 returns immediately
- Reproduced when running the above as root on a stock Fedora 44 (Incus system container) with `podman-5.8.9`
  - Also reproduced on `podman-6.3.0-dev`, installed from the [`rhcontainerbot/podman-next` copr](https://copr.fedorainfracloud.org/coprs/rhcontainerbot/podman-next/build/11232110/) (built from `d727bf2fc6a9c4e4993c6b7562f9553309395bb7`)

### Describe the results you expected

- Using `Notify=healthy` should only affect waiting for the container's health check to pass before sending its READY notification to systemd
- It should be possible to create and start other containers in the same pod during that waiting period

### Podman in a container

Yes

### Privileged Or Rootless

Privileged

### Upstream Latest Release

Yes

### Additional environment details

- Repro'd on Fedora 44 Incus system container (unprivileged, `security.nesting=true`) on an Ubuntu parent
- First encountered with `5.8.9` on Ubuntu 26.04

### Additional information

Originally encountered this because I have a quadlet pod with a distroless app container and a health check sidecar container (with `Notify=healthy`) whose health check probes the main app container. No ordering was defined between the two container units.

Running `podman auto-update` on the sidecar restarted the pod and the two containers were stuck crash-looping for >30mins as they hit systemd's timeout (the sidecar happened to continually win the start-first race). I added `After=app.service` to the sidecar unit as a workaround to mitigate the issue.
